authors: Preclinical studies have demonstrated the role of stress-induced dynorphin release in mediating a component of the anxiogenic and aversive effects of stress exposure. These results suggest that kappa opioid receptor (KOR) antagonists or low efficacy partial agonists may promote stress-resilience in humans and may potentially be useful in treating certain forms of mood disorders exacerbated by stressful experience. In rodent models; stress-induced stimulation of dynorphin release produces aversion; reduces open arm time; potentiates cocaine and nicotine conditioned place preference; inhibits social interaction and reinstates extinguished drug seeking. Each of these responses have been shown to be blocked by prior treatment with KOR antagonists or gene deletion of either KOR or prodynorphin. Two classes of KOR antagonists have been developed and clinical trials of both types have begun; but important differences in the molecular mechanisms of antagonism have been revealed. In addition; partial agonists that activate KOR without stimulating p38 MAPK may also effectively promote analgesia and stress-resilience. Understanding these ligand-directed signaling differences has important implications for the optimization of future therapeutics that manipulate the functioning of the KOR system to affect mood.
